articles.title: The surge of women elected in the 2026 midterms, particularly women of color, will shape political engagement for a generation of young people
paragraphs: On the day after the 2026 midterms, Atlanta’s WSB-TV led off its coverage by showing a series of almost entirely white men get replaced, one by one, by Black women .

Not only had Georgia elected Keisha Lance Bottoms as the nation’s first Black woman governor, African American women had also won positions as secretary of state, attorney general, state school superintendent, agriculture commissioner, insurance commissioner and labor commissioner.

In the legislative branch, Georgia’s likely incoming speaker of the House of Representatives is also a Black woman. Reporter Candace McEwen, herself a Black woman, ended her report by recounting how her 9-year-old goddaughter, upon seeing the graphic showing all the new Black women leaders in Georgia, commented, “I might have a shot!”

As political scientists who have long studied the effects of women politicians, our research has shown that both McEwen and her young goddaughter are right: When young people see politicians who look like them, they are inspired to be politically engaged .
Following the 2026 midterm elections, a record number of women will serve in state and national offices. More women of color will serve in prominent political offices than ever before.

As of this writing — with some races yet to be called — at least 162 women will serve in the U.S. Congress, 138 of them in the House of Representatives, according to the Center for American Women and Politics .

A minimum of 18 women will serve as governors, while 108 will serve in other statewide executive offices. The new Congress will seat an unprecedented 31 Black, 29 Hispanic, nine Asian American/Pacific Islander and four Native American women, and three women of Middle Eastern heritage.

These women of color will no doubt have significant effects on public policy as they draw on their life experiences while governing. In addition, our research shows that they will have another kind of impact on young people in their states and districts. Specifically, when women run for office, they motivate young girls to get involved in politics.

Women of color, however, are especially inspiring for young girls. Not surprisingly, they serve as role models for young girls of color, igniting their political interest and even leading them to envision themselves as running for office one day.

But their impact also extends to white girls, who are inspired by seeing these women overcome the double barriers of gender and race. This inspiration while young leads to greater political participation in adulthood .
There’s the concrete connection: Inspiration now, participation later.

While teenagers typically do not spend a lot of time following politics, they often absorb lessons from their political environment by osmosis, such as a news story shared on social media, passing by a billboard or holding a conversation with a parent or teacher. Because politics has historically been a man’s game – and a white man’s game at that – seeing women, and women of color especially, in public life changes their default assumption about who is suited to govern.

Politics is no longer just for white men. In the famous words of civil and children’s rights advocate Marian Wright Edelman, you can’t be what you can’t see . When young women see women in positions of leadership, they believe they can be leaders too.
If we left the story here, the election of all these women of color may seem like an unmitigated win for the long-term vitality of American democracy. But the story is a little more complicated.
The historic wave of women is a win for the future of the Democrats specifically. This is because the overwhelming majority of these newly elected women are Democrats.
Of the 162 women who have officially won their midterm House or Senate races so far, 122 – 75% – of them are Democrats . That’s a stunning party imbalance.

There is an even greater imbalance for women of color . In Georgia, all the African American women elected to statewide office are Democrats. In the U.S. House, all but four of the women of color are Democrats; in the Senate, it’s 100%.
This matters because we have also found that young people are most likely to see candidates from their own party as role models.

Lest you doubt that we can speak of teenagers as Democrats or Republicans, study after study finds that party attachments develop young, and the same polarization found among adults is mirrored in their children .

In other words, the girls who are inspired by this wave of women are far more likely to be Democrats than Republicans. Since partisan teens usually grow up to be partisan adults, this suggests that future Democratic women – whether they be racial minorities or whites – will be more politically engaged in adulthood.

For all the attention paid to the political choices of young Republican men, the party should be worried about the future of Republican women. Without more women politicians representing the GOP, Republican girls are likely to continue seeing politics as a man’s game and stay on the sidelines of civic life.
This doesn’t mean this wave of mostly Democratic women politicians won’t have any impact on Republican teens.
When women of either party run for office, both Republican girls and boys change their attitudes about women .

In general, Republican teens are less likely than Democrats to think that women have the necessary traits to be political leaders. But when they live in a community where women candidates run, they come to see women as fit to govern.
Why the change among Republicans and not Democrats? To be blunt, it is because Democratic kids do not need to be convinced that women are as capable of leadership as men.
Representation matters. We have found that barrier-breakers and firsts are particularly effective in changing young people’s beliefs and behaviors. The 2026 midterm elections produced many of those.
We expect that the effects will play out for years to come as more women believe that in politics, they have a shot.

articles.title: Who speaks for the voiceless in Tanzania?
paragraphs: ‘All we want is peace; there will be no peace without equal rights and justice.’

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “ Justice as infrastructure .” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL ) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here .
When courts stop protecting people, people stop talking. They stay quiet because speaking up could cost them their lives or their families. So who speaks for the voiceless?

In Tanzania, one answer comes with a guitar. Reggae artist Jhikoman, born Jhikolabwino Siza Manyika, has released a song called “Justice,” written for everyone who lost a loved one, and the right to mourn them out loud, after the October 2025 general elections that declared Samia Suluhu Hassan president.
“We don’t need no war, all we want is peace; there will be no peace without equal rights and justice.”

For nearly six decades, Tanzania cultivated an image of calm, consensus, and order. The scale of the 2025 election violence shocked many people because it broke that image. The BBC reported that security forces and unrest killed more than 500 people. International observers criticized the vote for its lack of transparency, and the African Union and the Southern African Development Community (SADC) said the election fell short of democratic standards.

“I was deeply moved by reports and accounts of people losing their lives, families losing their loved ones, and citizens being silenced by the authorities when they simply wanted to speak out, seek answers, and mourn those they had lost. That pain became my motivation to write ‘Justice.’”
This song is more than a song; it is a cry for humanity, a call for accountability, and a reminder that the pain of those who have lost loved ones should never be silenced.

Every stage name has a story, and Jhikoman’s is no different: JHIKO (from his first name, Jhikolabwino) plus MAN (from his surname, Manyika). Jhikoman has performed since 1994, blending acoustic reggae with African music and singing in English, Swahili, and his mother tongue, Kinyasa.

His musical life started at home. His older brother played guitar, and young Jhikoman watched, listened and dreamed. In secondary school, he fell for reggae, drawn by its messages of peace, love, unity, equality, and justice. He idolized Bob Marley and Alpha Blondy, and he covered their songs. Then his brother gave him the advice that changed everything: If you want to be a musician, write your own songs.

He took the advice to heart. In 1994, he stepped into a recording studio for the first time. In 2000, he released the album “Afro-Caribbean Beat,” and its title track became a local hit. The opportunities followed quickly. In 2001, he performed at the Zanzibar International Film Festival. In 2003, he wrote a song for Participatory Ecological Land Use Management (PELUM) Tanzania, an organization that supports small-scale farmers, and the commission took him to South Africa to perform at the World Forum for Sustainable Development. Since then, his music has carried him across East and Southern Africa and to stages in Europe.
“For me, music is more than entertainment. It is a powerful tool for communication, education, unity, and social change.”

“No innocent person should lose their life simply because of violence surrounding an election. The victims and their families deserve justice, dignity, and the freedom to mourn without fear or intimidation.”

According to Jhikoman, the people who spoke out and wanted democratic reform often got silenced. They called for changes to election laws and procedures that would guarantee free, fair, transparent, and credible elections. They also demanded equal opportunities for all political parties, independent electoral oversight, and the freedom to choose their leaders without intimidation.

Article 18 of Tanzania’s 1977 Constitution guarantees freedom of expression. Jhikoman says that some victims and their families have tried to enforce that right in court. However, getting justice has proved “extremely difficult.”

He points to several cases. After the alleged abduction of opposition activist Mpaluka Nyagali, known as Mdude, in May 2025, his wife filed a habeas corpus petition at the High Court in Mbeya. The court dismissed it on July 9, 2025, and his whereabouts remained unknown. A lawyer for former ambassador Humphrey Polepole filed a similar application after he disappeared in October 2025, and the court dismissed that as well.

Two advocates, Tito Magoti and Bob Wangwe, filed a case at the East African Court of Justice challenging the conduct of the election, and it remains pending. Authorities also arrested Tundu Lissu, chairman of the opposition party CHADEMA, and charged him with treason after he demanded electoral reforms. On November 6, 2026, the High Court acquitted him of treason, convicted him of incitement, and sentenced him to four years in prison. He remains imprisoned.

“The law guarantees freedom of expression, but people who criticize the government face arrest, intimidation, and, in some cases, alleged abduction. The central problem is not simply the absence of laws; it is the difficulty of holding those responsible for violations accountable.”

Listeners have responded well to Jhikoman’s message. He says that many Tanzanians feel the song finally carries their message to the international community. They believe the judiciary and parliament have lost their independence, which leaves them with little confidence that local institutions will deliver justice. Many now place their hope in international attention, because Tanzania has signed numerous international human rights agreements.
Some listeners also worry about his safety. They urge him to take care, since abductions and enforced disappearances remain serious concerns in parts of East Africa.

“I take those warnings seriously,” he says. “But I also believe that music can be a powerful tool for speaking out, raising awareness, and standing up for peace, justice, and the dignity of human life. … True peace means treating one another equally, standing up against injustice, respecting human rights, and giving everyone the freedom to express themselves without fear.”

Jhikoman’s story shows how justice shapes daily life long before anyone reaches a courtroom. When people trust that the justice system will treat them fairly and quickly, they speak out, report wrongdoings, and rebuild after loss. When they lose that trust, silence spreads. One reggae song cannot repair broken institutions, but it can name the problem, keep the memory of the dead in public view, and ask listeners to hold their leaders accountable.

articles.title: Guilfoyle resigns as ambassador to Greece – adding to the global vacancies sapping US embassies
paragraphs: The United States is down one more ambassador. On Oct. 13, 2026, it emerged that President Donald Trump had asked Kimberly Guilfoyle, a MAGA loyalist and ex-fiancée of Trump’s son Donald Jr., to resign her position as U.S. ambassador to Greece, a NATO ally. It follows allegations that the Trump adviser turned diplomat pushed for a Republican donor to pay off her six-figure American Express bill .

Guilfoyle later confirmed that she would comply with the request and resigned . In so doing, Athens became one of a number of U.S. overseas missions with a vacancy at the top. In fact, 93 out of 196 U.S. ambassador jobs are currently unfilled.

And that is after U.S. senators confirmed 10 new ambassadors before leaving town on Sept. 30, 2026. Among those nodded through before Congress closed for an extended midterm recess were new U.S. ambassadors for Kenya, Nicaragua, Malaysia and Kyrgyzstan.

With some of the vacancies the White House has not even sent names to Capitol Hill, despite the second Trump administration being a year and a half into the job. With others, the Senate, which is controlled by the same party as the White House, hasn’t acted on the names put forward. Should the Athens position be added to the list, the reason will be down to potential insufficient vetting or an ill-advised appointing strategy that promotes loyalty over experience.

Regardless of the reason, as a former ambassador and an expert in the process of diplomacy, I find the current vacancies concerning. Among those embassies still without a top person in place are key partners for the U.S. – countries that Washington needs to achieve its security, economic and strategic objectives.
What makes these vacancies more worrying, in my view, is that they come amid other concerning developments in the State Department’s staffing of embassies.

Chief among them are the high percentage of politically appointed ambassadors relative to positions filled by career diplomats – that is, senior foreign service officers, usually with at least 20 years of diplomatic experience.

Though many countries send politicians abroad as ambassadors, America’s diplomatic service is unique in two ways. The percentage of U.S. ambassadors who are political appointees – those who haven’t followed a career civil service path – is higher than comparative countries across the world. Second, those political appointees are often donors with little to no government experience .

The practice has existed for decades, but in recent years the number of political appointees has increased . During the Obama administration, the percentage of political appointees was around 30%. The number rose to around 40% in the first Trump administration and the subsequent Biden administration.
But in Trump’s second term, some 80% of names the White House has sent to the Senate have been political.

And many of the people Trump has put forward don’t appear to have the credentials usually associated with holding important diplomatic positions. Rather, many are friends, associates or donors to Trump, often with little overseas experience or knowledge of the country they are going to.

Lee Lipton, ambassador to a key ally in the Philippines, is owner of a restaurant in Palm Beach – Florida Benny’s on the Beach – a member of Trump’s Mar-a-Lago Club and a contributor to his political campaign.

The system of political appointees has always had an element of handing ambassadorships to friends and supporters. But what has changed under Trump is the range of positions now available. In the past, ambassadors to key countries like Chile, Israel, Peru, the Philippines, Turkey and Egypt, for example, have almost always been career appointees. This has changed under the second Trump administration.

Appointing noncareer diplomats to small, faraway nations has the additional problem that the chosen individual may not actually spend much time there. The rule of thumb has long been that ambassadors should spend no more than one month every year back in the United States. But that is compromised if a noncareer diplomat with expansive business ties in the U.S. is selected.
A closely related problem is the State Department’s handling of an ambassador’s second in command, their deputy chiefs of missions – DCMs for short – under Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

During Trump’s first term in the White House, politically appointed ambassadors were often encouraged to swap out the DCMs they inherited from their predecessors. It meant going through a long hiring process, leaving those key jobs unfilled for months.
In 2025, the State Department went further, canceling the assignments of senior officers en route to take up embassy jobs and opening a new hiring process.

It formed part of a Trump purge of what many MAGA Republicans characterized as a “deep state” civil service . The reality is that DCMs fill a critically important role in helping political appointees navigate the bureaucracy and implement their policy ideas, as well as raising the occasional reality check.
With more politically appointed ambassadors – some of them with no relevant experience – having an experienced DCM can be the difference between success and failure.
When you put all of these personnel changes together, the result is the degradation of what was once seen as one of the most effective diplomatic services in the world.

What makes this potentially more worrying is where the vacancies are. For example, Belarus and Bulgaria, neighbors to Russia and Ukraine, are without U.S. ambassadors. And important countries in the fight against terrorism or in geopolitical hot spots, such as Kuwait, Qatar and Mauritania, are in the same camp.

Other countries still without ambassadors include Indonesia, Southeast Asia’s largest nation and the most populous Muslim-majority country in the world; key Middle East ally Egypt and nuclear power Pakistan; and nations the U.S. needs to help manage inward migration, such us Haiti and Guatemala.

The problem of absent or inexperienced ambassadors goes both ways. It means Washington may not have a capable diplomatic figurehead in these countries to contact in times of need. There are also fewer avenues for host nations to successfully convey messages back to the U.S. administration.

When faced with absent ambassadors, amateurish political appointees and deputy mission chiefs who are very junior or career appointees with short resumes, host countries may conclude that they aren’t seen as important to the U.S. and start looking elsewhere for friends.

And the U.S. has hollowed out its ambassadorial corps at a time when it is facing growing international influence by the likes of Russia, China and Iran – rival nations hoping to capitalize on a perceived diplomatic void left by Washington.

articles.title: International Court of Justice rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people
paragraphs: This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “ Justice as infrastructure .” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL ) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here .

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled on November 19 that Myanmar’s military forces committed genocide against the Rohingya people during a brutal 2017 crackdown in the western Rakhine state.

Voting 9–6, the ICJ verdict found the military’s “clearance operations,” which led to the mass murder of at least 10,000 people and the forced expulsion of more than 700,000 Rohingya to the neighboring country of Bangladesh, constituted genocidal acts .

Myanmar has more than one hundred ethnic groups but refuses to recognize the Rohingya, who are considered illegal immigrants even though they were born in Myanmar, and many have been there for generations. The Rohingya have been viciously persecuted for decades and targeted by hate speech and violent acts not just by state forces but also by hardline Buddhist nationalists.
It was The Gambia, with the support of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, that initiated the ICJ complaint in November 2019.

This is the first time the ICJ has found a state liable for committing genocide. The Myanmar military government, which grabbed power in a February 2021 coup, described the decision as unfair and a “great disappointment” while pointing out that the verdict was not unanimous.
The National Unity Government of Myanmar, which represents the pro-democracy forces, said in a statement that the pursuit of justice cannot be realized without ending the junta rule.

“The ICJ judgment is an important step in the pursuit of justice, but it cannot be the end. Lasting peace requires accountability, protection for all communities and the dismantling of the structures that enable persecution and impunity.”

The ICJ ruling was eagerly awaited, especially by Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh. In one interview, 58-year-old Monajat Alam from one of the refugee camps shared, “The Myanmar military tried to convince the world that we had lied. Today, the truth has been recognized.”
Shwe Maung, a former Member of Parliament in Myanmar, emphasized that unity and national reconciliation cannot be achieved without recognizing the need to attain justice for the Rohingya.

As a former Member of Myanmar’s Parliament representing Buthidaung Township, I have long maintained that justice for the Rohingya and justice for the wider population of Myanmar are not competing causes.
Myanmar cannot build genuine federal democracy, national reconciliation, or lasting peace while denying grave crimes committed against one of its communities.
The Karen National Union, which represents the Karen ethnic community, reiterated the call to hold the Myanmar military accountable.

“The same Myanmar military that committed genocide against the Rohingya continues to commit atrocities against civilian communities across Burma. We must keep working together to bring justice to all the people of Burma who have suffered these crimes.”

The UN Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Myanmar, Kelley E. Currie, hailed the ICJ ruling. “Today the world court has called the crimes by their true name: genocide. That name matters. It is a recognition of what was done, and it puts us on the path to justice.”

The Special Advisory Council for Myanmar highlighted the call to sustain the verdict with decisive action. “Justice has been decided, but not yet delivered,” said Yanghee Lee, a founding member of the council.
Human rights activist Razia Sultana, who testified about the horrific violence endured by Rohingya women, asserted the urgency of ending the atrocities committed by the junta.
For the women who shared their testimonies with me, justice cannot remain only a judgment written on paper.
It must mean safety, recognition, accountability and the opportunity to rebuild their lives.
I think again of the women I met in the refugee camps, of what they described and the courage it took to speak.
Their voices travelled from the camps to the United Nations Security Council and became part of the wider international struggle for justice.
Thinzar Shunlei Yi shared the impact of the ruling on pro-democracy activists like her.
This verdict brings a sense of healing for me, too. It feels as though one of the chronic diseases Myanmar suffer has finally been named.
Having faced oppression myself as a woman and a political dissident, I know the scale of their suffering is incomparable—yet so many of us desperately needed to see that justice is possible.
Journalist Nyein Chan Aye is concerned over the recent rise of social media posts inciting hate against the Rohingya.

Rohingya civilians are not the enemies of Rakhine Buddhists, nor are Rakhine civilians the enemies of the Rohingya. Neither community is the enemy of Myanmar’s people. Their grievances and rights cannot be settled by another campaign of suspicion and hatred.

Around 14 countries have already acknowledged the ICJ ruling. Sanctions have been imposed as well by the United Kingdom government on senior military officers of Myanmar. Meanwhile, China raised the issue of “jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation” and warned that the ruling could undermine the settlement of disputes.

The junta remains in power, but pro-democracy forces are relentless in the struggle to restore civilian rule. Millions of stateless Rohingya are scattered in various camps, but the landmark ICJ ruling is a step forward in the pursuit of justice and the advancement of the demand to allow the persecuted minority to return to their home.

articles.title: Levent Alpöge
paragraphs: Levent Hasan Ali Alpöge (born April 1, 1992) is an American and Turkish mathematician. He is known for using artificial intelligence to resolve major unsolved problems in mathematics. Since 2024, he has been a member of the technical staff at Anthropic, an American AI company.

Alpöge was a junior fellow in the Harvard Society of Fellows before transitioning to the private sector. In 2025, he and collaborators gave a second proof that Hilbert's tenth problem has a negative answer over the ring of integers of every algebraic number field, a result first established the year prior.

On July 19, 2026, he presented an explicit counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture in three-dimensional space, stating that it was discovered using Anthropic's Claude Fable 5. In August, he announced a counterexample to the Carathéodory conjecture, and a positive answer to Hopf's problem concerning the existence of a complex structure on a 6-dimensional sphere. His AI-assisted work on Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness with Tristan Buckmaster was cited by OpenAI in their solution to the Millennium Prize Problem on September 8, 2026. The solution came under priority controversy after Buckmaster alleged that OpenAI had accessed his private work.

On November 20, 2026, Alpöge announced a proof of the generalized form of the Riemann hypothesis, another Millennium Prize Problem. It was formalized in the Lean proof language, developed with the assistance of an unreleased Anthropic model. The proof is not yet understood by mathematicians.

Alpöge was born on April 1, 1992, in Dix Hills, New York. He grew up on Long Island. His parents, Simay and Oğuz Alpöge, had immigrated to the United States from Turkey. He attended the Long Island School for the Gifted before studying at Half Hollow Hills High School West in Dix Hills, winning the Siemens prize as a high school senior.

He attended the Ross Mathematics Program at Ohio State University in the summers of 2007 and 2008, where he was first introduced to number theory. In 2010, Alpöge was a finalist in the Intel Science Talent Search for a computer-science research project conducted at Yale University on the algorithmic analysis of MRI scans of blood vessels. His earliest publication, on a CUDA-optimized vessel-detection method, dates from the same period. He also earned a Barry Goldwater Scholarship.

Alpöge attended Harvard University and initially considered studying computer science until taking and enjoying Math 55, an undergraduate mathematics course famous for its rigor. He studied algebraic number theory under Benedict Gross and spent summers doing mathematics research at Williams College under Steven J. Miller in 2012 and under Joseph Gallian at the University of Minnesota, Duluth in 2013. Alpöge received a Bachelor of Arts in mathematics and a Master of Arts in physics in 2014, winning a Hoopes Prize and being named to Phi Beta Kappa. He graduated summa cum laude and attained the highest GPA in his class. His undergraduate thesis, The average elliptic curve has few integral points, was supervised by Jacob Tsimerman, a Fields Medalist, and won the Captain Jonathan Fay prize for best senior thesis at Harvard.

After earning a graduate fellowship from the National Science Foundation, Alpöge studied Part III of the Mathematical Tripos at the University of Cambridge as a Churchill Scholar, earning a Master of Advanced Studies degree in 2015. He received a doctorate from Princeton University in 2020 with a dissertation titled Points on Curves, supervised by Fields Medalist Manjul Bhargava.

After completing his doctorate, Alpöge held an NSF postdoctoral fellowship affiliated with Columbia University and Harvard from 2020, and was a junior fellow in the Harvard Society of Fellows from 2021 to 2025. He subsequently joined the artificial-intelligence company Anthropic in 2024 as a member of the technical staff.

Alpöge works in number theory and arithmetic statistics, including the study of rational and integral points on elliptic and higher-genus curves, Selmer groups, and the distribution of arithmetic invariants of number fields.

With Manjul Bhargava and Ari Shnidman, Alpöge established the first proven bounds on the proportion of integers that can be written as a sum of two cubes of rational numbers. Their 2022 work showed that at most about five-sixths of integers are so expressible, combining geometry of numbers techniques with the circle method. The upper bound for the density of integers that are so expressible has been subsequently improved to 68.05% by Peter Koymans and Alexander Smith.

In a paper published in Inventiones Mathematicae in 2025, Alpöge, Bhargava, Wei Ho, and Ari Shnidman proved that for any quadratic extension of number fields K/F there exists an abelian variety over F of positive rank whose rank does not grow after base change to K. This implies that Hilbert's tenth problem has a negative solution over the ring of integers of every algebraic number field—that is, there is no algorithm to decide whether a polynomial equation has solutions in that ring. The result gave an alternative completion of a program relating Hilbert's tenth problem to the rank stability of elliptic curves and abelian varieties initiated by Bjorn Poonen, Barry Mazur, Karl Rubin, and Alexandra Shlapentokh; the Mazur-Rubin-Poonen-Shlapentokh program had been completed in 2024 by Peter Koymans and Carlo Pagano, using elliptic curves instead.

In July 2026, Alpöge announced on the social-media platform X that Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 large language model had found a counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture, a problem in algebraic geometry begun by Ludwig Kraus in 1884 and formally posed by Ott-Heinrich Keller in 1939. The example is a polynomial map from three-dimensional complex space to itself whose Jacobian determinant is the nonzero constant −2 but which is not injective, disproving the conjecture in dimensions three and above. The two-variable case of the conjecture remains open. The announcement was made outside of formal peer review, and the arithmetic of the example was independently checked by other mathematicians in the days that followed. This result was likely based on training data from a paper written by three other mathematicians.

On August 12, 2026, Alpöge announced on X that, together with Philippe Voinov and Saul Reynolds-Haertle and with help from Claude, he had constructed Hadamard matrices for all twelve orders below 2000 for which no such matrix had previously been known, namely 668, 716, 892, 1132, 1244, 1388, 1436, 1676, 1772, 1916, 1948 and 1964. Order 668 had been the smallest open case of the Hadamard conjecture since 2005.

articles.title: NASA’s CASALS Instrument Bridges Gaps in 3D Maps of Earth’s Surface
paragraphs: From orbit, today’s space-based laser instruments measure Earth’s forests and terrain one narrow line at a time. Between those lines are enormous gaps that include millions of acres of land scientists never directly measure. NASA’s CASALS instrument will blend machine learning with an ultra-compact lidar instrument to adaptively ‘sweep’ large swaths of Earth’s surface. This new capability for space-based remote sensors allows CASALS to create truly three-dimensional (3D) topographical renderings.
Video from a CASALS flight over the Great Cypress Swamp in Delaware on Nov. 12, 2024, showing tree canopy tops in green, the ground in purple, and near-ground vegetation in blue.

A team of researchers at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) has developed a new instrument designed to eliminate blind spots between lines of lidar data on the Earth’s surface. Built with support from NASA’s Earth Science Technology Office (ESTO), the Concurrent Artificially-intelligent Spectrometry Lidar System (CASALS) could help researchers map the features of Earth’s surface with unprecedented detail. Rather than mechanically steering a laser with moving mirrors, CASALS steers light using wavelength itself, generating a continuous, 3D swath of the ground below.

John Yorks, a physical research scientist at GSFC and Principal Investigator for CASALS, explained that the instrument features a novel transmitter and optical grating system that manipulates laser pulses without heavy, failure-prone motorized mirrors.

Instead, CASALS uses a fast-pulsing, tunable “seed” laser centered at 1040 nanometers, rapidly cycling through 256 unique wavelengths as it pulses through an optical component with a microscopic pattern of ridges called a transmission grating.

At this point, the physics of diffraction takes over. Because light bends at slightly different angles depending on its exact wavelength, the grating naturally “steers” each of the 256 pulses into a distinct position across the flight path.

This non-mechanical approach paints a continuous 3D swath of the ground. Not only does this eliminate the large unmapped gaps left between the isolated tracks of legacy spaceborne lidars, but stripping away moving parts drastically reduces the instrument’s size, weight, and power (SWaP) requirements. This makes it more reliable for the harsh environment of space.

Another key innovation within CASALS is its detector array. This component features a uniquely high Quantum Efficiency (QE), a variable that describes how effectively a detector converts incoming light (photons) into an electrical signal. CASALS operates at 80% QE. This means CASALS wastes almost none of the light that makes it back to the sensor.
With QE that high, CASALS can detect much weaker return signals, allowing it to collect useful measurements from darker surfaces or through denser vegetation.

This technology isn’t limited to a laboratory environment. In November 2024, an airborne CASALS prototype flew aboard NASA’s B200 King Air aircraft. The instrument produced science-quality datasets on its first campaign, exceeding the team’s expectations.

“I’m very impressed with Guang Yang, Jeffrey Chen, and all our engineers, and how well CASALS performed. This worked really well from the first time we flew it, which is pretty impressive,” said Yorks.
Flying at an altitude of roughly five kilometers, CASALS can distinguish individual tree branches and subtle changes in ground elevation, thanks to its 22-centimeter horizontal resolution.
“We’re able to see really fine details of vegetation structure and changes in the topography of the surface,” Yorks said.
The team aims to fly CASALS again as part of the Airborne Surface, Cryosphere, Ecosystem, and Nearshore Topography (ASCENT) campaign, scheduled for summer 2027.

But there’s more work to do to prepare the technology for space. The team plans to make several improvements to CASALS before creating a space-ready prototype. Specifically, they’re widening the instrument’s swath and adding onboard data processing software.
Transitioning from a successful airborne prototype to a fully realized space mission is a challenge, but the CASALS team is up to the task.

“The team’s really done a great job of sticking together and keeping on task and on schedule. We are being funded to optimize and improve the performance, and we’re also then looking at ways to take the technologies used in the airborne instrument and mature them and prepare them for a spaceborne version in the future,” said Yorks.

If successful, CASALS could become the first spaceborne lidar capable of mapping Earth’s forests and terrain as continuous three-dimensional swaths rather than isolated profiles, giving scientists a dramatically more complete picture of our changing planet.

articles.title: Oscar Wilde had a surprising rapport with Colorado miners – why it is hard to imagine that happening today
paragraphs: Oscar Wilde, the Victorian writer of “ The Picture of Dorian Gray ” and “ The Importance of Being Earnest,” was a fashionable icon known as much for his refined manner and conversation as for his writings.
So the image of Wilde exploring Colorado’s frontier towns and rugged mines sounds like a scene from a dream. But that is exactly what happened during his extensive tour of the U.S. in 1882.
Wilde arrived in the U.S. from Europe with much aplomb. The impresario Richard D’Oyly Carte, the promoter of the acclaimed operetta duo W.S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan, bankrolled Wilde’s tour.

Gilbert and Sullivan had recently written a new comic opera, “ Patience,” which mocked the aesthetic movement, of which Wilde was an icon. Championing artifice and refinement in all aspects of life, aesthetes dressed in ornate, unusual ways, such as Wilde’s habit of wearing an unnatural green carnation on his lapel. The often-mocked figure of the dandy, a wealthy man who dressed in the most bizarre and fanciful fashions of day, was an inspiration for aesthetes.

I study 19th-century literature in the English-speaking world, and I see Wilde’s western journey to my home state of Colorado as an example of how intellectual writers in the Victorian era were interested in the working class and how that curiosity was, perhaps surprisingly, mutual.

Carte brought Wilde to America around the time of the U.S. premiere of “Patience” to help popularize the idea of the aesthete. While on tour, Wilde visited major cities, such as New York and Philadelphia, giving almost 100 interviews . But he also was interested in the “Wild West.” His curiosity may seem paradoxical: Tawdry saloons and dusty main streets were a stark contrast to the atmosphere of luxurious refinement he cultivated.

Yet, above all, Wilde craved the novel and unexpected. He sought experiences and people who were the opposite of the conventionality he saw as chaining Victorian society. The slightly anarchic roughness of the West appealed to him. He called it “the most beautiful part” of the country.

Wilde arrived in Colorado Springs in April 1882 . Railroad baron William Jackson Palmer had founded this booming resort town in 1871 . The town, a short railway journey from Denver, served as a health retreat for those suffering from tuberculosis – one of the deadliest diseases in the nation at the time.

Befitting its growing popularity, Colorado Springs had a thriving arts scene. According to the Colorado Springs Pioneers Museum, “interest in the arts began almost immediately” and was distinguished by the opening of an opera house in 1881. Crafting it in red brick and sandstone, the architects took inspiration from Madison Square Theater in New York. It became one of the most impressive buildings in the state.

Wilde gave his lecture on “ The Decorative Arts ” at this opera house. He did not condescend to his Colorado audience, nor did he suggest that the highest quality art could only exist in the refined settings of Europe. Instead, he insisted that art should be a part of ordinary existence.

“Art,” he declared, “is not something which you can take or leave” but rather “a necessity of human life.” For Wilde, art meant “value to the workman” and “the pleasure which he must necessarily take in making a beautiful thing.” The quality of art for Wilde was not about luxury and extravagance but about creativity and honesty in creation.

The local paper, The Daily Gazette – now The Gazette – reviewed his talk positively in a column from April 15, 1882. The column praises Wilde for how “the entire evening he commanded the closest attention of his audience.” Reportedly, when he “would give expression to a brilliant thought or idea a murmur of applause would pass through the audience.” The article finishes by exclaiming that the lecture “was instructive and interesting and appreciated by all who were present.”
Wilde’s popularity in the West reveals the oversimplistic nature of the divide between the “highbrow” culture of the literati and the culture of “common” society.

His visit to the isolated, high-elevation mountain town of Leadville makes this blending of “high” and “low” culture even more vital. In this hardscrabble town, which owed its existence to the hard labor of miners, workers came to the Tabor Opera House to hear the lavish aesthete. Similar to his speech in Colorado Springs, he discussed how “beautiful and rational designs are necessary in all work.”
For Wilde, the roughness of his surroundings were closer to his ideal than the conventionality of Eastern U.S. cities, with their “bad wall-papers horribly designed.”
The relationship between Wilde and his Leadville audience was symbiotic. The artist found what he desired in the hard-edged mountain town, far from the pomp and conventions of Europe.
“The revolver was their book of etiquette,” Wilde wrote of the town, not altogether disapprovingly.
He drank with miners, some of whom lowered him into the depths of the Matchless Mine, a riotous atmosphere he found rather exciting.
The miners, he wrote in his “ Impressions of America,” were “very charming and not at all rough.” According to Wilde, these miners likewise found value in his discussions about art.

Newspaper articles about Wilde’s lectures in Colorado do not emphasize the cultural gap between him and his audiences. That dynamic may not have seemed odd – other than the novelty of a foreign celebrity visiting towns in the interior of the country.

In addition, 19th-century literary culture may not have conceived of the rigid divide between highbrow literati interests and those of the working class that exists today. The historian Lawrence Levine, in his influential 1990 book “ Highbrow/Lowbrow,” asserts that supposedly elite pursuits actually had wide appeal in 19th-century American culture.

For instance, opera was not associated primarily with multimillionaires in fancy tuxedos and evening gowns, but was also a popular pastime for all ages and social classes. That opera houses even existed in the frontier towns of Colorado demonstrates Levine’s point.
Working-class residents of Leadville appreciated the chance to hear Wilde lecture about art as much as he relished the chance to travel to a real mining town and talk with its residents.

In my view, economic and cultural divides of today can be bridged so everyone can engage intellectual insights and reflections. Witty, sophisticated authors like Wilde do not simply belong to exclusive elite circles.

articles.title: Powerhouse Parramatta: a museum of science, design and technology supercharged by spectacular art
paragraphs: There are so many published images of the new Powerhouse museum’s steel exoskeleton that it is hardly a surprise when two dazzling white structures like giant milk crates suddenly emerge from the depressing jumble of modern office buildings that characterise modern Parramatta.
But the light inside the building is something else, as glass walls invite the sky outside to come in.
Daylight is a key element in Overflow, one of the museum’s five opening exhibitions.

In a large open space with views to the Parramatta skyline and river below, a giant video screen plays a series of short films by Kamilaroi filmmaker Ivan Sen, showing seven different First Nations communities in New South Wales caring for their saltwater and freshwater country. Images of riverbanks, lagoons and sandy beaches are reflected in a shallow replica tidal pool in front of the screen.
Contemporary museums pride themselves on interacting with visitors, but this is the first time I have seen a museum encouraging people to wade into an exhibit.

According to the ceaseless political campaign against the Parramatta incarnation of the Museum of Applied Arts and Sciences, the original collection has been abandoned in favour of novelty. This is not true. Most of the works in The Dark, an exhibition specifically devised for children, come from the permanent collection.
Darkness here is a friend, not foe. Displays of beautiful minerals and precious stones are captioned with stories of the people who discovered them.

Those of us who are old enough to remember the eccentricities of the original museum in Ultimo can rediscover the pleasures of mechanical birds that sing with a pressed button, and the transparent woman whose body parts light up on command.
Another display features precious personal items lent by local children. Curatorship becomes community engagement.
The Powerhouse’s permanent collection also underpins The Mall, a celebration of the products, design and community life of the shopping mall.

There are arcade window displays and a re-imagined version of the beloved Raindrop Fountain inside Roselands shopping centre. Objects on display include an old-fashioned photobooth, antique cash registers and the original “Parramall” neon sign.

The David Jones archive, now a part of the Powerhouse collection and on display in the exhibition, includes mid-20th century advertising posters and photographs of window displays. It’s a window into a time when DJs was the epitome of style.
A commissioned series of portraits by photographers Jo Duck and Bahram Mia captures those who shop, socialise and work in today’s malls.

The largest and most hyped exhibition is Task Eternal, an exploration of flight – from a Burramattagal bumarang (boomerang) on loan from the British Museum to machines enabling exploitation of the moon.

The commissioned artworks include an immersive installation by American light artist James Turrell. The specially designed room evokes the disorienting Ganzfeld effect through an intense field of changing coloured light.
The curators, working with Chinese design firm OPEN Architecture, have created a nuanced investigation of wonder.

Leonardo da Vinci’s surprisingly fresh sketches of imagined flight sit alongside the Powerhouse’s collection of drawings and models by Australian aviation pioneer Lawrence Hargrave, who helped shape the 20th century’s achievement of an ancient fantasy.
There is an Apollo space capsule, aeroplanes and rockets, copies of messages sent with the Voyager craft on its endless journey into deep space, space suits – and space junk.
One of the most compelling exhibits is a digital display of the pollution now destroying the night skies, showing how this vandalism has taken less than a lifetime to “achieve”.

The fifth exhibition, The Turning, showcases recent works by British artist and designer Es Devlin, whose practice spans stage design, sculpture and installations, arena concerts by the likes of U2 and Lady Gaga, and large-scale events including the opening ceremony of the London Olympics.
The Turning opens with the Forest of Us, a meditation on organic symmetry. Visitors enter by walking past the sentence: “Every time I reach a fork in the road, I take both paths”.

These words lead visitors to a short, poetic film on the nature of organic symmetry. At the end of the film a door appears in the middle of the screen and the viewer walks into a giant mirror maze, beautiful and disorienting.
Never doubt that a small group of thoughtful, committed citizens can change the world; indeed, it’s the only thing that ever has.

In audio narration, Devlin lists places including the bus stop where Rosa Parks waited, the stadium stage where Martin Luther King spoke, the town hall steps where Greta Thunberg sat and the Block at Redfern, a key site of Australian First Nations activism.

In the next room, people are invited to sit at a long table for 15 minutes and draw a stranger opposite them, looking in their eyes without speaking. This work, titled Collective Portrait, is an actualisation of Devlin’s belief that the act of recording is a reminder that we are all part of a living universe.

On the lawn outside the Powerhouse, Devlin’s drawings of 244 endangered local species have been collaged into an egg-shaped stage. This forms the backdrop for Devlin’s performance work Come Home Again (first staged in London), featuring choral tributes to vulnerable species. The work will be performed at dusk from Thursday to Sunday during November, as part of the Powerhouse’s opening festival.
By any measure, Parramatta is lucky to be able to experience in depth the work of such a major art star.

“Powerhouse” has become a popular name for arts centres. Usually they are repurposed industrial buildings, made redundant by technological change. This Powerhouse is named in honour of its history and also, I suspect, in hopes of the impact it will have on both its surrounding suburbs and the wider community.
Powerhouse Parramatta is open 10am-5pm daily, and until 9pm Thursday-Sunday during November as part of its opening festival . Entry is free.

articles.title: Albanian Declaration of Independence
paragraphs: The Albanian Declaration of Independence (Albanian: Deklarata e Pavarësisë) was the declaration of independence of Albania from the Ottoman Empire. Independent Albania was proclaimed in Vlorë on 28 November 1912. Six days later the Assembly of Vlorë formed the Provisional Government of Albania which was led by Ismail Qemali and the Council of Elders (Pleqnia).

The success of the Albanian Revolt of 1912 sent a strong signal to the neighboring countries that the Ottoman Empire was weak. The Kingdom of Serbia opposed the plan for an Albanian Vilayet, preferring a partition of the European territory of the Ottoman Empire among the four Balkan allies. Balkan allies planned the partition of the European territory of the Ottoman Empire among them and in the meantime the territory conquered during First Balkan War was agreed to have status of the Condominium. That was the reason for Qemali to organize an All-Albanian Congress in Vlorë.
In Vlorë on 15/28 of the third Autumn 1328/1912.

After the words spoken by Mr. Chairman Ismail Kemal Bey, in which he told of the great danger Albania is in today, all the delegates with one voice decided that Albania today is to be on its own, free and independent.

Below is the list of the forty signatories as published by newspaper Perlindja e Shqipëniës. The original act of the Declaration of Independence was written on a single piece of letter. On the front page, there are a total of 34 recognizable signatures and on the back page are found 6 more signatures.

The National Assembly, composed of delegates from all over Albania and convening here in Vlora, opened today at four in the afternoon at the house of Xhemil bey. Ismail Kemal bey, as the prime initiator of the gathering, took the floor and explained to the delegates the purpose of the assembly, that is, that they all must strive to do what is necessary to save Albania from the great perils it is now facing.

The chairman, Ismail Kemal Bey, then took the floor and, in an ardent, fluid and reasonable speech, stated that although they had always been faithful to the Ottoman Empire, the Albanians had never forgotten their own language and nationality, the best proof of this being the endeavours and uprisings that had taken place from time to time, in particular over the last four years, to preserve their rights and customs. The Ottoman Government had never taken their interests into consideration and had never been willing to recompense the Albanians for the great services they had rendered. It had recently shown some interest in coming to an understanding with our people, but had not given proof of good faith and had not taken all the steps needed to appease and satisfy the Albanians. War had recently broken out with four countries in the Balkans that were seeking change and rights for their peoples, united by their ethnicity and religion.

Later, these countries put aside their initial objective and, as the war was going well for them, they agreed to divide the Empire up among themselves, including Albania. Realizing that the Turkish army had been defeated and that the Empire would not survive, the Albanians, who had played a greater role in the fighting than the soldiers, hastened to take requisite steps in their own interests as owners of the country. For this reason, Ismail Kemal bey departed for Istanbul and, having come to an understanding with the Albanians of Bucharest, too, set off for Vienna, where he reached an agreement with the Great Powers that had vital interests in the Balkans. As there was no more hope of saving Albania by means of arms, the only road to salvation was to separate Albania from Turkey. Ismail Kemal bey promoted this idea and objective, that was well received by all the Great Powers, in particular by Austria and Italy. It was only Russia that remained somewhat hostile to the idea because of the Slavs, but it did not deny the existence of Albania and an Albanian people. To realise this objective, he invited all Albanians to gather in Vlora and was delighted today to see that his call had not been in vain, and that delegates had been sent from all parts of Albania to reflect together on ways to save the Fatherland. According to Ismail Kemal Bey, the most urgent measures that the Albanian nation must take today are these: that Albania be independent under a provisional government; that a council of elders be elected to assist and supervise the government; and that a commission be sent to Europe to defend Albanian interests among the Great Powers.
The delegates unanimously agreed with the words of Ismail Kemal bey and resolved that Albania, as of today, should be on her own, free and independent under a provisional government.
The meeting was adjourned until the following day and the delegates went out and greeted the flag that was raised at five thirty in the afternoon.

The second session of the Assembly of Vlorë was held on 4 December 1912. During that members of the assembly founded the first government of Independent Albania on 4 December 1912, which was led by Ismail Kemal. The government established also a 'Council of Elders' (Pleqësia), which would help the government to its duties. In addition, the Assembly of Vlorë decided that it would agree to any decision of the Great Powers for the system of government in Albania and that the provisional government would cease to exist after the recognition of independence of the country and the nomination of the monarch.
The same day, Kemal waved the national flag of Albania, from the balcony of the Assembly of Vlorë, in the presence of hundreds of Albanians.

Just as the overseas communities of Albanians had stimulated the patriotic fervor which gradually led to the independence of their homeland, so at this critical juncture they once again demonstrated their solidarity. On 1 March 1913, they convened an Albanian Congress of Trieste, Austria. There were 119 representatives in all, coming from the United States, Romania, Bulgaria, Turkey, Egypt, Italy, and of course from the new state itself. Bishop Fan Noli of Boston was one of the featured speakers.

The congress recognized the provisional government of Ismail Qemal, pledged its faithful support, discussed the ethnic boundaries of the new state and sent strong resolutions to the European capitals and to the London Conference of Ambassadors then in session, appealing for their recognition of Albanian independence and for the lifting of the Greek blockade.

articles.title: Ottoman Empire
paragraphs: The Ottoman Empire, also known historically as Turkey or the Turkish Empire, was a state that spanned much of Southeastern Europe, West Asia, and North Africa from the 14th century to the early 20th century, centred in modern-day Turkey. It also controlled parts of southeastern Central Europe between the early 16th and early 18th centuries.

The empire emerged from a beylik, or principality, founded in northwestern Anatolia in c. 1299 by the Turkoman tribal leader Osman I. His successors conquered much of Anatolia and expanded into the Balkans by the mid-14th century, transforming their petty kingdom into a transcontinental empire. The Ottomans ended the Byzantine Empire with the conquest of Constantinople in 1453 by Mehmed II and claimed themselves as successors to the Roman Empire. Further conquests by Selim I led the Sultans to adopt the title of caliph. With its capital at Constantinople and control over a significant portion of the Mediterranean Basin, the Ottoman Empire was at the centre of interactions between the Middle East and Europe for six centuries. Ruling over diverse peoples, the empire granted varying levels of autonomy to its many confessional communities, or millets, to manage their own affairs per Islamic law. During the reign of Suleiman the Magnificent in the 16th century, the Ottoman Empire became a global power.

Modern academic consensus posits that the empire began to decline after defeat in the Second Siege of Vienna in 1683, but continued to maintain a flexible and strong economy, society and military into much of the 18th century. The Ottoman Empire fell behind technologically from the rest of Europe by the late 18th century as imperial authority fragmented. Further defeats from Austria and Russia culminated in the loss of territory, and with rising nationalism after the French Revolution, a number of new states emerged in the Balkans. Following Mahmud II's reign and the Tanzimat reforms over the course of the 19th century, the Ottoman state became more powerful and organised internally as a new Ottoman identity took hold. In the 1876 revolution, the Ottoman Empire attempted constitutional monarchy, before reverting to an absolute monarchy under Abdul Hamid II, following the Great Eastern Crisis.

Over the course of the late 19th century, Ottoman intellectuals known as Young Turks sought to liberalise and rationalise society and politics along Western lines, culminating in the Young Turk Revolution of 1908 led by the Committee of Union and Progress (CUP), which reestablished a constitutional monarchy. However, following the disastrous Balkan Wars, the CUP became increasingly radicalised and embraced Turkish nationalism, leading to a coup d'état in 1913 that established a dictatorship.

In the 19th and in the start of 20th centuries, persecution of Muslims during the Ottoman contraction and in the Russian Empire resulted in large-scale loss of life and mass migration into modern-day Turkey from the Balkans, Caucasus, and Crimea. The CUP joined World War I on the side of the Central Powers. It struggled with internal dissent, especially the Arab Revolt, and engaged in genocide against Armenians, Assyrians, and Greeks. In the aftermath of World War I, the victorious Allied Powers occupied and partitioned the Ottoman Empire, which lost its southern territories to the United Kingdom and France. The successful Turkish War of Independence, led by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk against the occupying Allies, led to the end of the Ottoman sultanate in 1922.

The word Ottoman is an historical anglicisation of the name of Osman I, the founder of the Empire and of the ruling House of Osman (also known as the Ottoman dynasty). Osman's name in turn was the Turkish form of the Arabic name ʿUthmān (عثمان). In Ottoman Turkish, the empire was referred to as Devlet-i ʿAlīye-yi ʿOsmānīye (دولت عليه عثمانیه), lit. 'Sublime Ottoman State', or simply Devlet-i ʿOsmānīye (دولت عثمانيه‎), lit. 'Ottoman State', and in Arabic, it was referred to as al-Dawla al-ʕaliyya al-ʕuṯmāniyya (الدولة العليَّة العثمانيَّة).

The Turkish word for Ottoman (Osmanlı) originally referred to the tribal followers of Osman in the 14th century. The word subsequently came to be used to refer to the empire's military-administrative elite. In contrast, the term Turk (Türk) was used to refer to the Anatolian peasant and tribal population and was seen as a disparaging term when applied to urban, educated individuals. In the early modern period, an educated, urban-dwelling Turkish speaker who was not a member of the military-administrative class typically referred to himself neither as an Osmanlı nor as a Türk, but rather as a Rūmī (رومى), or "Roman", meaning an inhabitant of the territory of the former Byzantine Empire in the Balkans and Anatolia. The term Rūmī was also used to refer to Turkish speakers by the other Muslim peoples of the empire and beyond.

In Western Europe, the names Ottoman Empire, Turkish Empire and Turkey were often used interchangeably, with Turkey being increasingly favoured both in formal and informal situations. This dichotomy was officially ended in 1920–1923, when the newly established Ankara-based Turkish government chose Turkey as the sole official name.

As the Rum Sultanate declined in the 13th century, Anatolia was a patchwork of independent Turkish principalities known as the Anatolian Beyliks. One of these, in the Bithynia region on the Byzantine frontier, was led by Osman I (d. 1323/4), a figure of obscure origin from whom the name Ottoman is derived. Osman's early followers were Turkish tribal groups and Byzantine renegades, not all of them Muslim. Osman extended his principality by conquering Byzantine towns along the Sakarya River, and a Byzantine defeat at the Battle of Bapheus in 1302 contributed to his rise. It is not well understood how the early Ottomans came to dominate their neighbours, due to a lack of sources. The Ghaza thesis popular during the 20th century credited their success to rallying religious warriors, but the idea is no longer generally accepted, and no other hypothesis has attracted broad support.

articles.title: NASA’s NG-25 Mission to Launch Pioneering Space Crops Research
paragraphs: NASA experiments, including a first-of-its-kind space crop production system, will travel to the International Space Station aboard Northrop Grumman’s 25th Commercial Resupply Services mission for the agency.
Investigations from NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division will advance research that benefits life on Earth and future exploration, expanding knowledge of space crops and human health.

Astronauts will need sustainable sources of food to travel farther and stay longer in space. To help understand how crop production works in microgravity, NASA is launching a novel space crops growth chamber called Ohalo III.

The new prototype growth chamber will provide critical insights for developing safe, nutritious, and reliable crop production strategies for future Moon Base habitats and Mars missions. Knowledge gained from the space crop production system also could help inform agricultural practices such as vertical farming and indoor growing systems.
Researchers will validate the system’s water delivery and volume optimization technology aboard the space station.
A precision health investigation is the next step toward enabling long-duration studies of human brain tissues in space.

The research builds on a previous investigation that sent small, lab-grown models of the human brain, called miBrains, to the space station. This experiment will validate a miniature fluid-handling system designed to mix, deliver, and maintain the nutrient-rich liquid needed to keep the tissues alive.

Researchers could use the findings to help identify potential neurological risks associated with spaceflight and develop strategies to protect astronaut health. It also may advance human tissue research and neurological disease modeling on Earth.

NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division pioneers scientific discovery and enables exploration by using space environments to conduct investigations not possible on Earth. Studying biological and physical phenomena under extreme conditions allows researchers to advance the fundamental scientific knowledge required to go farther and stay longer in space, while also benefitting life on Earth.

articles.title: Indiana-class battleship
paragraphs: The Indiana class was a class of three pre-dreadnought battleships launched in 1893. These were the first battleships built by the United States Navy comparable to contemporary European ships, such as the British HMS Hood. Authorized in 1890 and commissioned between November 1895 and April 1896, these were relatively small battleships with heavy armor and ordnance that pioneered the use of an intermediate battery. Specifically intended for coastal defense, their freeboard was insufficient to deal well with the waves of the open ocean. The turrets lacked counterweights, and the main belt armor was placed too low to be effective under most conditions.

The ships were named Indiana, Massachusetts, and Oregon and were designated Battleship Number 1 through 3. All three served in the Spanish–American War, although Oregon—which was stationed on the West Coast—had to cruise 14,000 nautical miles (26,000 km; 16,000 mi) around South America to the East Coast first. After the war, Oregon returned to the Pacific and participated in the Philippine–American War and the suppression of the Boxer Rebellion, while her sister ships were restricted to training missions in the Atlantic Ocean. After 1903, the obsolete battleships were decommissioned and recommissioned several times, the last time during World War I when Indiana and Massachusetts served as training ships, while Oregon was a transport escort for the Siberian Intervention.

In 1919, all three ships were decommissioned for the final time. Indiana was sunk in shallow water as an explosives test target a year later and sold for scrap in 1924. Massachusetts was scuttled off the coast of Pensacola in 1920 and used as an artillery target. The wreck was never scrapped and is now a Florida Underwater Archaeological Preserve. Oregon was initially preserved as a museum, but was sold for scrap during World War II. The scrapping was later halted and the stripped hulk was used as an ammunition barge during the battle of Guam. The hulk was finally sold for scrap in 1956.

The Indiana class was very controversial at the time of its approval by the United States Congress. A policy board convened by the Secretary of the Navy Benjamin F. Tracy came up with an ambitious 15-year naval construction program on 16 July 1889, three years after the Maine and the Texas were authorized. The battleships in their plan would include ten first-rate long-range battleships with a 17 knots (31 km/h; 20 mph) top speed and a steaming radius of 5,400 nmi (10,000 km; 6,200 mi) at 10 kn (19 km/h; 12 mph)—6,500 nmi (12,000 km; 7,500 mi) maximum. These ocean-going ships were envisioned as a possible fleet in being, a fleet capable of raiding an enemy's home ports and intended to deter powerful warships from ranging too far from home. Twenty-five short-range second-rate battleships would provide home defense in both the Atlantic and Pacific and support the faster and larger long-range vessels. With a range of roughly 2,700 nmi (5,000 km; 3,100 mi) at 10 knots and a draft of 23.5 ft (7.2 m), they would roam from the St. Lawrence River in the north to the Windward Islands and Panama in the south and would be able to enter all the ports in the southern United States.

It was proposed, probably for cost reasons, that the short-range battleships should have a hierarchy of three subclasses. The first would mount four 13-inch (330 mm) guns each on eight 8,000-long-ton (8,100 t; 9,000-short-ton) ships, the second would mount four 12-inch (305 mm) guns each on ten 7,150-long-ton (7,260 t; 8,010-short-ton) ships, and the third would mount two 12-inch and two 10-inch (254 mm) guns each on five 6,000-long-ton (6,100 t; 6,700-short-ton) ships. The two battleships already under construction, Texas and Maine, were to be grouped under the last class. In addition, 167 smaller ships, including rams, cruisers and torpedo boats, would be built, coming to a total cost of $281.55 million, approximately equal to the sum of the entire US Navy budget during the previous 15 years (adjusted for inflation, $6.6 billion in 2009 dollars).

Congress balked at the plan, seeing in it an end to the United States policy of isolationism and the beginning of imperialism. Even some supporters of naval expansion were wary; Senator Eugene Hale feared that because the proposal was so large, the entire bill would be shot down and no money appropriated for any ships. However, in April 1890, the United States House of Representatives approved funding for three 8,000-long ton battleships. Tracy, trying to soothe tensions within Congress, remarked that these ships were so powerful only twelve would be necessary instead of the 35 called for in the original plan. He also slashed the operating costs of the Navy by giving the remaining Civil War-era monitors—which were utterly obsolete by this time—to navy militias operated by the states. The appropriation was also approved by the Senate, and in total three coast-defense battleships (the Indiana class), a cruiser, and a torpedo boat were given official approval and funding on 30 June 1890.

The first class of short-range ships as envisioned by the policy board were to mount 13-inch/35 caliber and new 5-inch (127 mm) guns, with 17 in (432 mm) of belt armor, 2.75 in (70 mm) of deck armor and 4 in (102 mm) of armor over the casemates. The Indiana class, as actually built, exceeded the design in displacement by 25 percent, but most other aspects were relatively similar to the original plan. An 18-inch (457 mm) belt and a secondary battery of 8-inch (203 mm) and 6-inch (152 mm) guns were adopted, the latter because the Bureau of Ordnance did not have the capability to construct rapid-firing 5-inch weaponry. The larger weapons were much slower firing and much heavier, but without the bigger guns, the ships would not be able to penetrate the armor of foreign battleships.

The Indiana-class ships were designed specifically for coastal defense and were not intended for offensive actions. This design view was reflected in their moderate coal endurance, relatively small displacement and low freeboard, which limited seagoing capability. However, they were heavily armed and armored, so much in fact that Conway's All the World's Fighting Ships describes them as "attempting too much on a very limited displacement." They resembled the British battleship HMS Hood, but were 60 ft (18 m) shorter and featured an intermediate battery consisting of eight 8-inch guns not found in European ships, giving them a very respectable amount of firepower for their time.

articles.title: Controversial Netflix hit The Body blends 2000s nostalgia, Catholic satire and queer longing
paragraphs: As far as TV episode titles go, you would be hard-pressed to find many more inflammatory than “Slutty God”. Opening Netflix’s new hit show The Body, the provocation neatly sets the tone for the unholy antics of the rebellious Catholic schoolgirls at the centre of the drama. At the same time, it encapsulates the divisive response that has embroiled the series.

The Body has been both praised by many queer viewers for its portrayal of lesbian desire, and condemned by over 100,000 petitioners for what they dub “blasphemous” content. But for fans of queer cinema, The Body’s artfully crafted opposition between Catholicism and sapphism, God and the gays, is nothing new. The film industry has long used this seeming incompatibility as a point of tension.

In featuring implausible visions, hyperbolic satanic panic and improvised rituals within a Catholic high school, The Body combines the established cinematic themes of isolated community and satirical blasphemy. One group exorcism devolves into hilarity as schoolgirls each confess their deepest sins – “I’m not a natural blonde!”, “I’m part of the fucking chess club!”, “I masturbate to Daddy Franklin [the school’s resident priest]!” The scene removes all the power from the moralistic structures that demand their piety.

Set in the 2000s, The Body pairs a nostalgic soundtrack with a heavily rhinestoned wardrobe . It features a lesbian storyline between Anya (Kristina Bogic) and Elise (Sara Boustany), the popular co-captains of the Catholic high school’s all-girl dance team.
Rather than disparaging Christianity, The Body’s ethereal dance numbers and hypnotic party montages reimagine queer girlhood as an alternative to institutional religion.

These scenes capture what film studies researcher Catherine Wheatley identifies as an emerging tradition of “postsecular” cinema. That is, works that play with the boundaries between belief and unbelief, questioning both the certainty of the theist and the atheist. That approach offers “enchantment, awe and wonder without the politicising constraints of traditional religious faith”.

In what is quickly becoming one of the show’s most beloved scenes, Anya and Elise perform an emotional dance duet to Jeff Buckley’s Lover, You Should’ve Come Over. The camera revolves around the two actors as the surrounding spotlights are successively switched off. The dark background increasingly contrasts against their all-white costumes and plunges the couple into an otherworldly bubble.

It’s a transcendent experience in which the girls move in unison in a way that enables them to lose track of their social inhibitions. The awe on display here is not for God, but for the gut-wrenching, all-consuming power of a queer teenage crush.

On-screen portrayals of Christianity and queerness have seen a notable surge in the past decade. Many films showcase the inner turmoil of a closeted protagonist, often within an insulated religious group, as in You Can Live Forever (2022).

Others intensify that conflict by focusing on so-called “conversion therapies” . Examples include Boy Erased (2018), Fair Haven (2016) and The Miseducation of Cameron Post (2018). The latter stars The Body’s creator Quinn Shephard as Cameron’s girlfriend.

But I’m A Cheerleader (1999) is perhaps the most iconic lesbian conversion drama. It bridges two popular approaches in queer Christian films: stories about conversion therapy and comedies that mock religious homophobia rather than leaning into heavy drama.

Falling loosely within this category, the nunsploitation trend of the 1970s has found a renaissance in The Little Hours (2017) and Benedetta (2021). Both films feature lesbian themes in their irreverent critiques of Christianity and power.

This boom in queer religious media seems to be symptomatic of the progressively increasing influence of Christian nationalism on politics, particularly in the US. Some of the 21st century’s most heated debates have revolved around the role of religion in shaping legislation. Key examples include the overturning of Roe v Wade in 2022 and the rollout of various anti-trans measures since Donald Trump’s re-election.

As partisanship deepens and the far right gains ground, growing numbers of Republicans are embracing ideas aligned with Christian nationalism . Meanwhile, Democrats face pressure to shift further to the right, a dynamic that both fuels and appeases rising anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment across the US .

The petition calling for The Body to be cancelled claims that “Netflix would never do this to Muslim or Hindu families”. That argument only reinforces the link between the backlash against the series and an idealised vision of a white, heteronormative Christian nation. A nation often framed by Trump’s rhetoric as being under threat .

Through its creative choices, Shephard’s series directly challenges the assumption of Christian dominance that anchors this worldview. Displacing the centrality of Catholic belief systems through a humorous irreverence and a transcendent queer desire, The Body manages to offer political critique while packaging it all in a highly marketable aesthetic.

Ultimately, the show turns what critics call blasphemy into something joyful, stylish and hard to ignore. It’s a reminder to viewers that queer desire needs no permission from tradition to feel sacred.
